In a project that uses ES modules, a `require()` or `module.exports` written out of habit mixes two module systems. Bundlers can't tree-shake anything that's loaded with `require()`, and the other `import/*` rules can't check names that are exported through `module.exports`.

A `require()` is reported if it has one string as its argument and isn't inside a function. By default it's also allowed inside an `if`, a `try`, a `? :` or an `&&`, `||` or `??`, because an `import` declaration can't be conditional.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. To turn it on:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"import/no-commonjs" = "error" # or "warn"
```

Every option, set to its default:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"import/no-commonjs" = ["error", {
  allowRequire = false,
  allowConditionalRequire = true,
  allowPrimitiveModules = false,
}]
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 2} */}
```js
const { parse } = require("./parse");

module.exports = { run: text => parse(text) };
```

{/* bad */}
```js
import { parse } from "./parse";

exports.run = text => parse(text);
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
import { parse } from "./parse";

export const run = text => parse(text);

let colors;
try {
  colors = require("colors");
} catch {}

export function loadMarkdown() {
  return require("markdown-it");
}
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowRequire` | `false` | Allow every `require()`. `module.exports` and `exports.*` are still reported. |
| `allowConditionalRequire` | `true` | `false` also reports a `require()` inside an `if`, a `try`, a `? :` or a logical expression. |
| `allowPrimitiveModules` | `false` | Allow `module.exports = value` if the value isn't an object literal. |

The string `"allow-primitive-modules"` instead of the object means `{ "allowPrimitiveModules": true }`.

{/* good {"options": [{"allowRequire": true}]} */}
```js
const { parse } = require("./parse");

export const run = text => parse(text);
```

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowConditionalRequire": false}]} */}
```js
let colors;
try {
  colors = require("colors");
} catch {}

export { colors };
```

With `allowPrimitiveModules`, a module may export one function or one string:

{/* good {"options": [{"allowPrimitiveModules": true}]} */}
```js
module.exports = function run(text) {
  return text.trim();
};
```

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowPrimitiveModules": true}]} */}
```js
module.exports = { run };
```

## When not to use it

Leave it off in a project that's written in CommonJS, and for config files that a tool loads with `require()`.
